strengths: Extremely simple and practical contribution: MINTO requires only a few lines of code, no new hyperparameters, and negligible computational overhead, making it immediately adoptable across many off-policy RL algorithms.

Unusually broad and careful empirical evaluation: the method is tested in online and offline RL, discrete and continuous control, and across value-based (DQN), distributional (IQN), conservative (CQL), and actor-critic (SAC with SimbaV1/V2) frameworks, on 15 Atari games, 14 Atari offline datasets, and 26 continuous control tasks, with IQM and confidence intervals over 5-10 seeds.

Thoughtful ablation study (Fig. 1, 19, 20) comparing the minimum operator against Online Only, Target Only, Max, Mean, and Random, which directly supports the design choice and demonstrates that Max fails due to overestimation, empirically answering both stated research questions.

Fair benchmarking against the most relevant prior baselines (Double DQN, FR-DQN, ScDQN, Maxmin DQN), rather than only vanilla target networks; MINTO beats them while using fewer parameters than Maxmin DQN.

Theoretical grounding: convergence of the tabular MINTO operator is proven as a special case of the Generalized Q-learning framework (Lan et al., 2020), with the non-expansion verification in Appendix A.

Good analysis of mechanism: the online selection ratio curve (Fig. 4 right) shows the target network dominates early and the online estimate is used ~45% of the time later, illuminating how the method behaves.
Strong reproducibility practices: shared codebase, JAX code snapshot, detailed hyperparameter tables, per-game breakdowns in the appendix, and use of public datasets and standard protocols.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core idea (taking a minimum between two Q-estimates to curb overestimation) is a small variant of well-established techniques (Double Q-learning, TD3's clipped double Q, Maxmin Q-learning); the contribution is primarily an empirical demonstration rather than a new principle.

Gains are uneven across settings: improvement on IQN is modest (~7%), performance on DMC-Hard is comparable or slightly lower with SimbaV2, and some per-game results (e.g., VideoPinball, Qbert with CNN) show no clear advantage or overlap in confidence intervals, weakening the claim of 'consistently improving performance'.

The convergence analysis is largely derivative: it is a straightforward verification that MINTO fits Assumption 1 of Lan et al. (2020) and only covers the tabular case, offering little new theoretical insight into why min(online, target) works under function approximation.

Evaluation does not disentangle the two claimed mechanisms (moving-target mitigation vs. overestimation bias reduction) - e.g., no measurement of estimation bias over training or comparison with a weighted/adaptive combination that could trade off conservatism, which the authors themselves flag as future work.
Only 5 seeds for most Atari experiments is on the low side for distinguishing the reported AUC gaps (e.g., 7-18%), and no formal statistical tests are provided beyond confidence intervals.

The full codebase is 'shared upon acceptance' rather than included, limiting full reproducibility at review time, and experiments are confined to established benchmarks with no multi-task, multi-agent, or real-robot settings despite the claim of broad applicability.

Some design choices are under-justified, e.g., using a single critic for SAC+MINTO (the twin-critic variant is relegated to the appendix and reportedly performs worse), which complicates interpreting whether the gains stem from the architecture change or from MINTO itself.

strengths: The proposed change (element-wise minimum between online and target network estimates in the bootstrap target) is simple, well-motivated, and can be dropped into many off-policy algorithms with negligible overhead, as demonstrated by pseudocode and a JAX snippet.

The empirical evaluation is broad in coverage: value-based (DQN), distributional (IQN), offline (CQL on RL Unplugged), and actor-critic continuous control (SAC with SimbaV1/V2 on MuJoCo, HumanoidBench, DMC-Hard), using modern evaluation practices (IQM, stratified confidence intervals, per-game breakdowns in the appendix).

The operator ablation (min vs. max vs. mean vs. random vs. online-only vs. target-only) directly tests the design choice, and the analysis of the online-selection ratio over training gives some insight into the method's behavior.
Related work is thorough and the positioning relative to Maxmin Q-learning, Double DQN, FR-DQN, and ScDQN is clearly articulated.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core contribution is a one-line modification (min over online and target Q-values). This sits very close to well-known ideas—Double Q-learning's min-style overestimation correction, twin-critic SAC (which already takes a min over two online critics), Maxmin Q-learning, and TQC-style conservative targets. 'Take the minimum of two estimates' is arguably an obvious first thing practitioners would try; the paper provides no principled argument for why this specific pairing of networks is the right one beyond the empirical ablation.

The theoretical contribution is thin: Corollary 1 is a direct special case of the Generalized Q-learning framework of Lan et al. (2020), and the proof (two-line verification of non-expansion) is routine. It also only covers the tabular setting, offering no insight into the deep RL dynamics the paper is actually about.

The choice of the minimum operator is justified purely empirically (Fig. 1) on 15 Atari games with 5 seeds; there is no analysis of when or why min helps (e.g., underestimation in low-noise regimes, interaction with exploration, per-game variance). The authors themselves concede in the conclusion that the trade-offs are 'not yet understood.'

Gains are modest and inconsistent across settings: ~18% AUC over vanilla DQN, but only ~7% over IQN, comparable (or slightly negative on DMC-Hard) for SimbaV2, and clear gaps only for the weakest baseline (vanilla CNN DQN). On several Atari games the curves are within noise of the baselines. The improvements over Maxmin DQN, which trains an ensemble, are not always clean per-game (Fig. 12 shows Maxmin winning on several games).

The offline CQL results are hard to attribute: adding min between online and target critics increases conservatism, and the huge gains (~125% AUC on CNN) may largely reflect extra pessimism rather than 'faster learning from fresher estimates'; no analysis (e.g., Q-value magnitude tracking, sensitivity to alpha) disentangles this.

Statistical support is weak for the breadth of claims: only 5 seeds for Atari experiments and baseline comparisons, with IQM confidence intervals that overlap for many method pairs, yet the text repeatedly claims 'consistently outperforms.'

The operator ablation compares a heterogeneous set of alternatives (random selection, mean, max) but omits other natural competitors, e.g., a convex combination tuned as a hyperparameter, or min with the target only on a delayed schedule, which would test whether the benefit is really about 'fresh online estimates' versus simply added pessimism.

strengths: Simple, practical, and well-motivated contribution: the MINTO update rule (minimum between online and target network estimates) is easy to implement, hyperparameter-free, and nearly free computationally, making it immediately useful to practitioners.

Extensive and well-structured empirical evaluation across a wide range of settings: online discrete control (DQN, IMPALA+LN), distributional RL (IQN), offline RL (CQL on RL Unplugged), and continuous control (SAC with SimbaV1/V2 on MuJoCo, HumanoidBench, DMC-Hard), with consistent aggregate gains (e.g., ~18-24% AUC improvement for DQN variants).

Good ablation study on the selection criterion (Fig. 1 and Appendix D.5): systematically compares min against max, mean, random, and target-only/online-only, providing empirical support for the design choice rather than presenting it as arbitrary.

Thoughtful benchmarking against closely related methods (Double DQN, FR-DQN, ScDQN, Maxmin DQN) with clear discussion of how MINTO differs, and a nice analysis of the online-selection ratio over training (Fig. 4 right).
Theoretical grounding: convergence of MINTO is established via the Generalized Q-learning framework of Lan et al. (2020), with a complete verification of the non-expansion conditions in the appendix.
Good reproducibility practices: shared JAX codebase, detailed hyperparameter tables per setting, pseudocode for all integrations, code snapshot, and a stated intent to release the full codebase.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: taking a minimum of network estimates to control overestimation is a well-known idea (Double Q-learning, TD3's clipped double Q, Maxmin Q-learning). The core contribution is applying this operator between the target and online networks, which is a relatively small conceptual step; the paper is more of a careful empirical study than a new method.

Small number of seeds (5) for most Atari experiments weakens statistical strength of the claims, especially given the substantial variance visible in several per-game plots; 10 seeds are only used in the continuous-control setting.

Some claims of consistency are overstated relative to the evidence: results are not uniformly positive (e.g., SimbaV2+MINTO is slightly worse on DMC-Hard, several HumanoidBench tasks show degradation or overlapping confidence intervals, and Qbert/MsPacman show mixed results for DQN+MINTO). The conclusion honestly acknowledges this, but the abstract's 'consistently improves' framing is stronger than the data.

The theoretical analysis is limited to the tabular setting via an existing framework and does not explain why min outperforms mean or random combination, which would strengthen the principled argument; the work is essentially empirical in its justification.

Potential interaction with exploration and pessimism (acknowledged in the conclusion) is not investigated, and no adaptive operator selection baseline is compared, which is a natural alternative the paper itself proposes as future work.

Offline RL gains for CQL+MINTO are surprisingly large and somewhat at odds with the intuition that more conservative targets would slow learning; while a plausible explanation is offered, the mechanism is not analyzed in depth.

strengths: The proposed MINTO update rule is simple, hyperparameter-free, and requires negligible compute overhead, yet the paper demonstrates remarkably broad applicability across DQN, IQN (distributional RL), CQL (offline RL), SAC with SimbaV1/V2, and CrossQ+WN, spanning online/offline and discrete/continuous settings.

The empirical evaluation is extensive and follows modern best practices: IQM aggregate metrics with confidence intervals, 5 seeds on Atari (per-game breakdowns in appendix), 10 seeds on continuous control, and an ablation over alternative combination operators (Max, Mean, Random, Online Only, Target Only) that directly justifies the design choice of the minimum operator.

The paper benchmarks against relevant and well-chosen baselines that also leverage online estimates (Double DQN, FR-DQN, ScDQN, Maxmin DQN), rather than only comparing against vanilla target networks, which strengthens the claim that the minimum-based selection criterion is the key ingredient.

The tabular convergence analysis via the Generalized Q-learning framework of Lan et al. (2020), while a corollary, provides theoretical grounding, and the Appendix E bias analysis on Car-on-the-Hill (100 seeds, ground-truth Q*) provides mechanistic insight into how MINTO trades off overestimation bias against learning speed.
Good reproducibility: public code release, complete pseudocode for all integrations, detailed hyperparameter tables, and standard evaluation protocols (Machado et al. 2018, RL Unplugged datasets).
weaknesses: The core contribution is conceptually incremental: taking the minimum of online and target estimates is a small design change closely related to Clipped Double Q-learning (Fujimoto et al., 2018) and a special case of the Maxmin Q-learning framework (Lan et al., 2020), on which the theoretical result also relies; the novelty rests primarily on the empirical demonstration rather than a new idea or analysis.
The theoretical contribution is a direct corollary of prior work and is limited to the tabular setting; no analysis addresses function approximation, where the method is actually used.

Results are not uniformly positive: gains on DMC-Hard are comparable or slightly negative for SimbaV2, and in the offline setting Maxmin CQL (N=2) outperforms MINTO, requiring the authors to combine MINTO with Maxmin to recover the advantage—this somewhat weakens the claim of a general-purpose improvement.

The acknowledged risk of systematic underestimation/over-conservatism in low-noise environments is not deeply analyzed, and the interaction with exploration is left as future work; an adaptive variant is not explored.

Five seeds per Atari game is on the lower end, and the paper lacks a rigorous statistical significance analysis (e.g., performance profiles with stratified bootstrap comparisons) for the aggregate claims across benchmarks.

strengths: Technically sound core idea: the proposed target update (min of online and target network estimates) is simple, hyperparameter-free, and costs only one additional feedforward pass, making it easy to integrate into many off-policy algorithms.

Extensive and fairly broad empirical evaluation: online discrete control (DQN, Double DQN, Maxmin, ScDQN, FR-DQN), distributional RL (IQN), offline RL (CQL and variants on RL Unplugged), and continuous control with SAC/SimbaV1/V2 and CrossQ+WN, with per-task breakdowns and standard IQM/statistical reporting.

A thoughtful operator ablation (Min vs. Max, Mean, Random, Online-only, Target-only) that directly supports the design choice, plus a nice empirical analysis of estimation bias on Car-on-the-Hill with ground-truth values.

Convergence in the tabular setting is formally established via the Generalized Q-learning framework of Lan et al. (2020), and the paper is transparent about trade-offs (e.g., potential over-conservatism in low-noise environments).
Good reproducibility: public code, hyperparameter tables, pseudocode for all integrations, and standard evaluation protocols (Dopamine, RL Unplugged).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: taking a minimum of value estimates to curb overestimation is well established (Clipped Double Q-learning, Double Q-learning, Maxmin Q-learning). The core contribution is essentially applying this operator between the target and online networks of a single estimator, which reads as an incremental tweak rather than a principled new insight.

The convergence result is a straightforward corollary of existing theory (Maxmin/Generalized Q-learning) with a two-page verification; it adds little beyond prior work and does not address function approximation, which is the practically relevant regime.

Empirical gains are modest and inconsistent in the most modern settings: improvements over IQN (~7-10%) are relatively small, DMC-Hard results are comparable or slightly worse for SimbaV2, and improvements shrink substantially with stronger architectures (IMPALA+LN), suggesting the benefit may diminish as baseline stability improves.

Only 5 seeds for most Atari experiments and sensitivity of results to the choice of 15/14-game Atari subsets weakens statistical strength; per-game results show several settings where gains are within noise or negative (e.g., some offline tasks in Figs. 14-17).

Underlying mechanisms are not fully understood: the paper acknowledges that MINTO may be overly conservative, that it may dampen optimistic estimates needed for exploration, and that its interaction with exploration is 'not yet fully understood' — an important gap given overestimation bias is the entire motivation.

The claimed advantage over Maxmin DQN (better performance with less compute) is confounded: Maxmin with N=2 was reportedly worse in online Atari but better in offline CQL, and the authors' explanation (conservatism vs. exploration) is speculative without supporting ablations.

Overall significance is limited: the method is a useful practical trick, but it is unlikely to reshape research directions in deep RL, and the contribution may be better suited to a workshop or shorter venue.

strengths: The proposed method (MINTO) is extremely simple and lightweight: a one-line modification to the TD-target computation that introduces no new hyperparameters and negligible overhead, making it trivially adoptable and highly reproducible.

The evaluation is unusually broad and thorough for a paper of this kind: online discrete control (DQN, IQN on Atari with two architectures), offline RL (CQL on Atari), and online continuous control (SAC with SimbaV1/V2, CrossQ+WN) across MuJoCo, Humanoid Bench, and DMC-Hard, with consistent positive results in most settings.

The paper includes a principled ablation (Section 4.2, Appendix D.7) comparing the minimum operator against Max, Mean, Random, Online-Only, and Target-Only alternatives, directly justifying the design choice rather than only demonstrating end-to-end gains.

Comparison against relevant prior baselines (Double DQN, FR-DQN, ScDQN, Maxmin DQN/CQL) is conducted rather than only comparing against vanilla target networks, and the paper transparently reports where Maxmin CQL outperforms in the offline setting.

Convergence of the tabular operator is established via the Generalized Q-learning framework of Lan et al. (2020) with a clean, verifiable proof, and an additional bias analysis on Car-on-the-Hill against a precomputed ground-truth value function strengthens the empirical claims.

Code, pseudocode for all integrations, hyperparameter tables, per-game breakdowns, and a reproducibility statement are provided; standard evaluation protocols (Machado et al. 2018, Dopamine, RL Unplugged) and IQM with confidence intervals are used throughout.
weaknesses: The core idea has limited conceptual novelty: taking the minimum of two bootstrapping estimates closely echoes the Clipped Double Q-learning trick (Fujimoto et al., 2018) and Maxmin Q-learning (Lan et al., 2020), and the hybrid online/target construction is close to ScQL (Zhu & Rigotti, 2021) and FR-DQN; the contribution is primarily an empirical recombination rather than a new mechanism, which is acknowledged but not deeply differentiated.

The min is taken between two highly correlated networks (the target is a lagged copy of the online network), which is fundamentally different from the independent-critic setting where min-based bias correction was originally justified; the paper does not provide an analysis of when this correlated minimum systematically biases the value estimates (e.g., persistent underestimation), relying instead on the empirical bias study.

Results are not uniformly positive: on DMC-Hard, MINTO is comparable (SimbaV1) or slightly worse (SimbaV2), and Maxmin CQL with N=2 notably outperforms MINTO offline, requiring MINTO to be added on top of Maxmin to recover the advantage, which weakens the 'consistently improves' framing.

Theoretical contribution is incremental: convergence follows as a direct special case (N=1, K=2) of the existing Maxmin framework, so it mainly confirms the operator is a non-expansion rather than providing insight into deep RL behavior.

Several experiments use only 5 seeds, which is on the low end for Atari; some conclusions (e.g., the 7-22% AUC improvements) would be more convincing with more seeds or stratified bootstrap significance tests.

The acknowledged limitations (possible over-conservatism in low-noise environments, unexplored interaction with exploration, reliance on a fixed update period T that governs the online/target selection dynamics) are left unanalyzed; a study of how the online selection ratio varies with T would substantially clarify the method's behavior.
